La patrouille du Quartier chinois est-el: Is the Chinatown patrol a good way to protect the community?
Craignant pour la sécurité de sa communa: Fearing for his community’s safety, Jimmy Chan decided to take matters into his own hands.
Depuis le début de la pandémie de COVID-: Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020, Montréal’s Asian communities have been hit hard by the rise of anti-Asian racism. Chinatown, where foot traffic has dropped sharply, has been the scene of vandalism and attacks against Asian people. Fearing for his community’s safety, Jimmy Chan decided to take matters into his own hands. In mid-April, together with his friend Eddy Li, this Chinese-Montréal community leader formed a security patrol that protects the neighbourhood several days a week.
Est-ce que cette patrouille protège vrai: Does this patrol really protect the community? La Converse went to Chinatown to find answers. On June 29 at 8 p.m., Chinatown is teeming with life. Hit hard by the pandemic, this colourful neighbourhood is gradually returning to its usual rhythm – people sip bubble tea, enjoy Cantonese dim sum and catch up with friends. A lively atmosphere fills the air. On De La Gauchetière, the main pedestrian thoroughfare, community elders greet each other with smiles, restaurant owners swap the latest news about their businesses, and young people gather around their latest food finds.
On pourrait presque croire que la vie es: You could almost believe life has returned to normal in the neighbourhood, if it weren’t for the two men in police-style uniforms at Sun Yat-Sen Park.
<strong>« Si on le fait pas, qui le fera: “If we don’t do it, who will do it for us?”
Sur le coin sud-ouest du parc, Eddy Li e: On the park’s southwest corner, Eddy Li and Jason, two professional security guards, stand ramrod straight, ready to step in at the first sign of trouble. “In September, the racism became intense. In total, we spent more than 500 hours on volunteer patrol,” says Mr. Chan. Dressed in a sharp jacket and perfectly pressed black pants, he proudly wears his title of Chinese community leader, with a Chinese pin on his left lapel.
Il est si connu et respecté dans la comm: He is so well known and respected in the community that several passersby greet him and ask to take photos with him. According to him, the neighbourhood’s merchants are very grateful. “Some of them work until 11 p.m., and our patrol walks them to the metro station. They’re very happy,” Mr. Chan says with delight. “When they don’t see us, they ask me where I am. They thank us by giving us free meals.”
D’après lui, ces commerçants ont été vic: According to him, these merchants have been victims of numerous acts of vandalism and hate crimes. Along the way, Mr. Chan chats with several of them, who congratulate him on his work, including the owners of Buffet Jade and Restaurant Cuisine Cantonaise. They talk cheerfully in Taishanese and Cantonese about how the patrol has helped their businesses.
M.Chan nous conduit aussi devant différe: Mr. Chan also takes us past various shops that have had their windows smashed and been robbed, describing in detail what happened.
On s’arrête longuement devant la grande: We stop for a long while in front of the big red sign of Sammi & Soupe Dumpling, a restaurant known for its xiao long bao. “This restaurant’s windows were broken. Homeless people made huge holes in them in broad daylight!” he laments. In front of the restaurant, a small sign on a silver pole says there is a security camera near the restaurant. Yet no camera can be seen. “I remember someone who did a news interview and said there was no camera at this spot and that one should be installed. There still isn’t one!” exclaims a young woman standing right next to us. Rebecca Ng could easily blend into the evening crowd in Chinatown. But this recent graduate in security techniques has come to take a training session offered to the team’s new patrollers.
Un incident raciste l’a poussée à se joi: A racist incident pushed her to join the team. “A racist man on the metro turned to me and yelled, ‘F*** China! F*** Japan!’ I took out my camera and filmed him,” she says, outraged. “I filed a complaint against him in criminal court. The criminal case is still before the court. I really want to see this case through to the end.”
Cette confrontation s’est produite en ma: This confrontation happened last March at around 9:30 p.m., as the young woman was leaving the Chinatown pastry shop where she worked at the time. Ms. Ng was already thinking of changing careers and moving into security, because her jobs at a pastry shop and a bubble tea shop were not stable and did not allow her to make a decent living.
L’incident a renforcé sa décision. « Je: The incident reinforced her decision. “I want to join the patrol to mobilize for my community. If we don’t do it, who will do it for us? I’m lucky not to have children or heavy responsibilities, so I can take the time to do this properly,” she says. After hesitating, she tells us that the desire to serve her community is not the only thing motivating her. “I know I’m very lucky, because I wasn’t hurt and I managed to film a video. But I wish I had defended myself more, because I just sat there and asked him to stop,” she adds with regret.
Ce n’est pas tout le monde qui voit la p: Not everyone sees the patrol as an effective solution to the area’s safety problems. On May 27, 2021, the blog mychinatownmtl published <l1>an article</l1> about the police presence in Chinatown that sent shockwaves through the Chinese community. The blogger who wrote the post, who prefers to remain anonymous for fear of harassment, does not believe a patrol is the best way to keep the community safe. According to mychinatownmtl, increased surveillance of the area is not ideal, because police are used against racialized people.
« Ils ont l’air de nous protéger, mais b: “They look like they’re protecting us, but many past cases have shown that it doesn’t work. For example, during the 1992 Los Angeles riots, in Koreatown, the police presence only made things worse,” the blogger explains. The blogger also points out that the police are a problem for the large homeless population in the area. “The police give them more fines and chase them out of Chinatown. That kind of action is harmful to building a healthy relationship between our two communities,” the blogger says. “I’m really afraid they’ll bring in anti-loitering laws that target these populations.”
These fears are not unfounded. After an hour of patrolling, we return to Sun Yat-Sen Park. This park is a place where Mr. Li has had a lot of problems.
« S’il y a des gens qui dorment ici, c’e: “If people are sleeping here, it’s loitering. Loitering is when people are in a place and aren’t doing anything. Sleeping in the park is loitering, because the park isn’t meant for that,” he explains. When he sees people sleeping in the park, he directs them to the nearest shelter, which is farther down the same street. If they need medical care, Mr. Li calls emergency services. Another spot favoured by Chinatown’s homeless population is the alley behind the Kam Fung restaurant. We stop in front of a dark space surrounded by concrete blocks. The area inside the perimeter formed by the blocks is filled with white mattresses, blankets and pillows.
Il n’y a encore personne dans ce campeme: There is no one in this encampment yet. Mr. Li points to a square heat vent on the wall of the building running alongside the encampment. “Homeless people and people with drug addictions like to hang out here, because they can stay warm near this vent,” he explains. “The problem is that they leave a lot of garbage and it ends up spilling into the street. Also, it’s not safe for them to be there, because if they lie down in the alley, they can be hurt by passing cars.” For these reasons, the police have tried many times to move them to shelters. They showed up with big trucks to haul them all away. “It doesn’t look great when the authorities move them, but at the same time, it will help homeless people be in a better place.
Ils vont pouvoir recevoir l’aide médical: They’ll be able to get the medical and social help they need,” Mr. Li reasons. “I understand they have nowhere to go, so I tell them to go to the shelter. They have free spaces. Homeless people just don’t want to go. I don’t know why, maybe they just have something against the system or they had a bad experience.” The homeless people who frequent this encampment do not seem to share his view. Mr. Chan confirms that several were shocked that their home was gone. Unwilling to go to shelters, they came back to the same spot and rebuilt their encampment.
Pour eux, c’est un lieu de rassemblement: For them, it is a community gathering place. They often hold parties and barbecues there. mychinatownmtl thinks it knows why homeless people distrust shelters. “Since last year, homeless people haven’t wanted to go to shelters because there are COVID-19 outbreaks there. So they’re always on the street, surrounded by hostile architecture. One of the only places they can sleep is in Chinatown.”
Plusieurs membres de la communauté chino: Several members of the Chinese community believe the patrol is not a lasting solution and only worsens relations between the Chinese community and the neighbourhood’s homeless community. These people are looking for more lasting solutions that address the root of the problem and build bridges between the two communities. “Personally, I take a social approach, because in my view, the elements of criminality are social elements,” says May Chiu, a lawyer and member of Chinois progressistes du Québec. “Punishing people because they’re criminals, as the patrol does, is saying there’s no hope of reintegrating them into society.”
Me Chiu défend plutôt une approche préve: Chiu instead advocates a preventive approach that aims to directly tackle the social causes of crime. In other Montréal neighbourhoods where merchants have similar anxieties about crime and homeless people, solutions that work for everyone have been put in place. “If they see someone stealing inside, these merchants say, ‘Sir, ma’am, I’m not going to call the police, but I can pay you $10 if you clean up here.’ This approach allows these people to take care of life’s necessities,” Chiu points out. Other businesses have also offered free meals to people who were trying to steal from them.
L’avocate croit que cette solution perme: The lawyer believes this solution creates bonds between merchants and homeless people that can help fight crime. According to her, if bonds of trust are built between a homeless person and a business that often gives them food, that person will be more likely to alert those around them when the business is being vandalized, in order to protect it.
Le Quartier chinois de Toronto a adopté: Toronto’s Chinatown has adopted a similar strategy to fight crime. Friends of Chinatown Toronto (FOCT), an anti-gentrification organization in Toronto’s Chinatown, has partnered with Community Fridges Toronto to ensure food security for people in the area. At the corner of D’Arcy Street and Spadina Avenue, in the heart of Chinatown, they have installed a fridge where everyone can access healthy food.
« On ne voudrait pas encourager les gens: “We wouldn’t want to encourage people to call the police or to depend on the state. We have more community-based measures. They’re not directly linked to preventing hate crimes, but when the community is more connected, there’s more trust between people,” says Florence Yee, a member of FOCT. “There’s more than one aspect to community safety. When we started, during the pandemic, it was about distributing masks, food security and housing security.” One of the measures put in place to build these bonds of trust is the Phone Tree.
Deux membres de FOCT sont responsables d: Two FOCT members are in charge of this phone line service, which responds to the community’s urgent needs. Currently, the Phone Tree serves as an information resource on COVID-19 and vaccination. This measure is complemented by two vaccination ambassadors on the ground, who share information in English, Mandarin and Cantonese. “A community’s safety isn’t only about preventing hate crimes, but also about health in general,” Florence explains.
